say.en: Stand dominoes in a long line. If the first one falls, and each falling domino always knocks over the next, then every domino falls, however long the line. In this lesson: State the principle of mathematical induction.
Prove formulas for sums by induction.
Explain why both steps are needed.

body.en: Let P(n) be a statement about natural numbers. If (1) P(1) is true (the base case) and (2) whenever P(k) is true, P(k + 1) is also true (the inductive step), then P(n) is true for every natural number n. In the step we assume P(k) (the *induction* hypothesis) and use it to prove P(k + 1). The base may start at any n₀; then the result holds for all n ≥ n₀.

points.en: Both together ⇒ P(n) for all n

Base case: n equals 1. The left side is 1, the right side is 1 squared.
Assume P k: the sum of the first k odd numbers is k squared.
Add the next odd number, 2k plus 1, to both sides.
That is P k plus 1. By induction, P n holds for all n.

problem.en: Prove by induction that 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.

steps.en: Assume Σ to k = k(k + 1)(2k + 1)/6. Add (k + 1)².

answer.en: True for all natural numbers n

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Prove by induction that 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Prove by induction that 1 squared plus 2 squared plus... plus n squared equals nn plus 12n plus 1/6.
n equals 1: 1 equals 1 times 2 times 3 over 6 ✓.
Assume Σ to k equals kk plus 12k plus 1/6. Add k plus 1 squared.
= k plus 1[k2k plus 1 plus 6k plus 1]/6 equals k plus 1(2k squared plus 7k plus 6)/6 equals k plus 1k plus 22k plus 3/6, which is Pk plus 1.
So the answer is True for all natural numbers n.
